extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in comedy/festival news, comedians, venue operators and industry observers
extracted.subtask_description: A news report about the cancellation of a comedian's Fringe show that outlines reactions and the debate over offensive material, venue responsibility, audience expectations, and free-speech concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue acceptability / alignment with values
rubrics_metrics.description: The material presented must be acceptable and align with the venue's values; the venue will not present shows whose material it finds unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasance: 'The Pleasance is a venue that champions freedom of speech and we do not censor comedians’ material. While we acknowledge that Jerry Sadowitz has often been controversial, the material presented at his first show is not acceptable and does not align with our values. This type of material has no place on the festival and the Pleasance will not be presenting his second and final show.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue responsibility vs free-speech claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming to 'champion freedom of speech' does not prevent a venue from withdrawing association with material it deems unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights a tension: the Pleasance states it 'champions freedom of speech' and 'do[es] not censor comedians' material' yet canceled the show because it 'does not align with our values' — showing venues balance free-speech principles against reputational/ethical responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience expectation and informed consent / promotional warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences may be warned by promotional material that a show could be offensive, and patrons should be given fair notice to decide whether to attend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotion quoted Sadowitz: 'Please note that I might just do card tricks and say nothing for a whole hour or I might just do the usual 'screaming fascist' schtick. Or both. Patrons may wish to drink alcohol pre-show to avoid boredom, embarrassment and guilt.' This exemplifies transparency about potentially offensive content and managing audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer track record influences tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedian's history of increasingly offensive gigs or established persona affects how audiences and venues receive and tolerate material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeremy Vine: 'Each gig was more offensive than the last. No one complained because that's what Jerry does.' Prior reputation can explain why some audiences expect offense and why reactions vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between offensive material and indefensible content
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a boundary between material that is merely offensive (part of a comedian's persona) and content deemed 'indefensible' that justifies stronger responses like cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience member: 'It was his indefensible content.' The article implies evaluators must judge whether jokes, comments, or acts cross from provocative to indefensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-consensual or physically indecent on-stage behavior is unacceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical acts toward audience members (e.g., indecent exposure or other non-consensual behavior) are treated as beyond acceptable comedic offense and can trigger cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cited in reporting: 'He got his penis out to a woman in the front row.' The audience member framed that as part of 'indefensible content', indicating physical/non-consensual conduct is a separate, disqualifying issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedian community solidarity and protest tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Fellow comedians may publicly support a performer facing cancellation and may adopt protest tactics (e.g., reproducing the contested material) as a form of resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simon Evans: 'If you can identify the line that got you cancelled then I for one am willing to nick it. And I think every other comic should too. This is our Spartacus moment.' Other comics expressed public support, demonstrating industry norms of solidarity and protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellations situated in broader cultural/free-speech debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions to cancel are often interpreted through wider political/cultural lenses (e.g., 'woke' culture vs. traditional free-speech concerns), affecting public reaction and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leo Kearse: 'If the Islamic fundamentalists don't get you, the wokeists will.' Many comments in the article frame the cancellation as part of ongoing culture-war arguments about toleration and censorship.
